Money is your material. 
Give it shape.

This week, Mercury launched real-time payments: money that lands in seconds, any hour, any day, for free. Product Manager David Hill, and Product Designer Jen Pearce on what it took to make that real ↓

The hardest part wasn't just building the rail. It was competing with muscle memory. ACH and wires have had decades to become the default. Your recipient's details are already saved. You've paid them this way before. Real-time payments had to earn that same familiarity from scratch.

Mercury's job was to make the fastest option the easiest one, too. Before you even choose, we pre-check whether your recipient's bank accepts instant payments and prefill their payment details where we can. When the best option is available, it's already in front of you.

"Most banks haven't made instant payments free or easy for businesses," says David.

Real-time payments are live this week for eligible Mercury Business and Personal accounts. Free, instant, and yours to use today.

Our Treasury customers moved into two new mutual fund products, each over a single weekend, and it was so seamless almost nobody noticed. 

Fund migrations can take months and cause disruption along the way. For cash that businesses use to run payroll and pay vendors, that wasn't an option — so before Trevor J. Walters and the Investments team could launch the new offerings, they spent most of a year rebuilding what sits underneath them.

Reference data for every investment asset Treasury supports lived across 13 tables and 32 files. The team replaced it with a Security Master Service, creating a shared source of truth for market data, trading systems, and the Treasury ledger. Adding or changing an asset went from about a month of engineering work to one Ops instruction. "It's one of those critical pieces where nobody notices when it's working but everyone feels it when it's missing," Trevor said.

They also moved Mercury Treasury and Mercury Personal Invest onto Ascend, Apex's new real-time custodian infrastructure. Trading, account management and money movement now run on modern, real-time APIs instead of a legacy overnight batch system. This unlocked faster account opening and faster wire settlements into Treasury, so we can move as quickly as our customers do.
 
Then came the migrations themselves. Holdings moved from the old funds to the new ones over one weekend each, and customers logged in Monday to new, Mercury-exclusive funds that were already invested.

The unglamorous work is usually the real work. More on how this came together and what it unlocks for your business: https://lnkd.in/gmBm3Q7V

Real life doesn't run on banking hours. Your payments shouldn't either.

That's why we've launched real-time payments on Mercury Business and Mercury Personal.

Now you can move money in seconds, day or night, weekend or holiday, and it's free on both.

So, whether you're paying someone at 9pm on a Friday or settling an invoice the moment it's due, whatever day that happens to be, you'll get confirmation right away.

If you didn't know instant, always-on payments were even possible, now they are. Free and 24/7 for eligible Mercury Business and Personal accounts.

Startups have never held this much cash. Global venture funding topped $500 billion in the first half of this year alone, and most of it sits parked in an account.

Founders are usually left choosing between two options to put the cash to work / to invest it: take on more risk for a better rate, or play it safe and leave return on the table. We wanted a better option for our customers.

Brand Designers Sarah Mohammadi and Serena E. spent weeks on one texture. Not the color, not the shape. Just how it would feel against your thumb.

Mercury's IO card, designed by artist Simone Bodmer-Turner, shipped last week. A sculpture is a three dimensional object, layered, catching light from a dozen angles. A card is a flat rectangle that has to survive a wallet. Translating from sculpture to product is where the two designers spent most of their time.

Bodmer-Turner leaves her materials in whatever natural state they settle into, a patina, a rough edge, a surface that was never smoothed over. "It feels natural, as if it has always existed," Serena said. Getting that same quality onto something flat meant treating the card's surface itself as the material. "We wanted to go beyond adding an image of something special. We wanted to make people feel like they're holding a piece of art."

It started with how the sculpture was photographed. Sarah and the team studied every shadow and highlight in the reference shots, since a flat, evenly lit photo would have erased exactly the depth they were trying to preserve. Then came the detail almost nobody would guess took the longest: the crop, worked through what Sarah called "countless iterations to get the right balance of detail and abstraction."
